v.why: Raising an already large learning rate (toward 1.0) causes divergence, whereas at low or mid rates the same step helps or is neutral.
At very small learning rates the network is undertrained in 243 epochs, so a larger step size boosts accuracy.
Lowering a divergent-level learning rate restores stable training, unlike at low or mid rates where it slows learning.
With a low learning rate, bigger batches mean fewer updates and more undertraining.
Smaller batches give many more Adam updates, which helps when the learning rate is too small to converge.
Small batches add gradient noise and more steps at a high learning rate, increasing instability.
Wider layers amplify the effective update size, so a high learning rate becomes more unstable.
At a low learning rate, wider networks fit faster and are less undertrained.
Deeper ReLU networks are more prone to divergence at high learning rates.
Increasing an already strong L2 penalty (toward 1) underfits, while small alpha changes are nearly neutral.

The main ideas are that a high learning rate makes training unstable, and that a low learning rate leaves the model undertrained, so the number of update steps matters.
